title: Ground and soil
summary: The ground is covered with grass over soil: a mixture of broken rock, dead plant material, water, air and living things. Zoom into the block of soil by the oak to see inside it.

layers.basics: Soil is not just dirt. It holds grains of rock, the remains of dead plants and animals, water, air and an enormous number of living things, from earthworms to microbes. Plant roots anchor in it and drink from it. In this park a block of soil 1.2 metres deep has been cut open beside an oak, so you can see its layers, its stones and roots, the fungal threads and the burrow of an earthworm, and the animals that live in it. Choose "The soil under your feet" in the list of parts to go there.
layers.deeper: Soil grains clump together with the help of humus (dark decayed material), clay, plant roots and fungal threads, and the gaps between the clumps hold air and water. Fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and release nutrients that plants take up. Tree roots reach out through the soil with the help of fungal partners (mycorrhiza). Under the high ground of Greenwich Park lies a pebbly sand, the Blackheath pebble beds, with clays and chalk deeper below.
layers.expert: The soil block is a model built from typical measurements: the rock below is what the geological survey describes for the Greenwich Park plateau, and the depths of the soil layers are typical, not measured. The park around it is a simplified scene, not a scan of a real place. Away from the block, zooming into the grass shows a simplified generic view of soil grains and organisms, not a sample of real soil.

facts: 1.5 m across, 1.2 m deep, by the oak

title: The soil under your feet
summary: A cut block of park soil 1.5 m across and 1.2 m deep, standing where the lawn meets an oak's roots: layers of soil and rock, stones, roots, fungal threads, crumbs, and the animals that live in it.

layers.basics: Soil is the thin skin of the Earth where rock, air, water and living things meet. This block shows it as if the lawn had been cut open with a spade 1.2 metres deep. Under the grass comes a dark layer rich in dead plant material, then a darker, crumbly topsoil full of roots, then a paler subsoil, and at the bottom the pebbly sand that the soil grew from. Across all of it run oak roots, white fungal threads and the burrow of an earthworm, and in the surface layers live animals from a ground beetle to springtails smaller than a grain of rice. Choose a layer with the buttons: Surface, Topsoil, Subsoil, Whole profile cut, Life only (the soil turns see-through so only living things show) or Open the earthworm. Click anything to read about it, and zoom into the crumb or the clay to see what the soil is made of.
layers.deeper: Soil is a mixture of mineral grains (sand, silt and clay), dead and decaying organic matter, water, air and a very large number of living things. About half of a typical soil by volume is solid and about half is pore space, shared between water and air. The layers are called horizons, lettered O, A, B and C from the top down; this block draws all four. The soil of the Greenwich Park plateau forms in the Blackheath pebble beds, a layer of sand and rounded flint pebbles that lies at the top of the park. The block is a typical lawn soil, not a core from the park: the rock below is what the geological survey describes, the depths of the soil layers are typical values, and the animals, roots and stones are placed for illustration. Soils on these beds elsewhere south of London are mapped as acid, sandy soils, so the real soil is probably paler and sandier than a textbook loam.
layers.expert: How the picture was made: every solid part is a closed mesh cut by a plane, so you see a true section of each horizon, stone, root and worm. Sizes are real where they are known and are stated on each card (the earthworm 170 mm by 8 mm, the woodlouse 15 mm, springtails 1.8 mm, oribatid mites 0.7 mm). Not to scale: fungal threads are drawn about 40 times thicker than the real 4 to 6 micrometre hyphae so that they can be seen, the density of grass blades, roots and crumbs is illustrative, and the colours on the cut face are a code. The park is itself a simplified scene, so this is not a core taken at a particular spot in Greenwich Park.

title: The soil profile: horizons O, A, B and C
summary: A soil profile is the vertical section through a soil, from the surface down to the rock it grew from; its layers, called horizons, are lettered O, A, B and C.

layers.basics: If you dig a pit, the soil is not the same all the way down. Soil scientists name the layers with letters. O is the surface layer made of dead plant material (leaves, grass thatch). A is the topsoil, where mineral grains are mixed with dark, decayed organic matter and where most roots and animals live. B is the subsoil, paler, with less living matter. C is the loose rock or sediment that the soil grew from, hardly changed. In the Whole profile cut view you can see all four with their typical depths.
layers.deeper: The letters follow the international descriptions of soil horizons: O is organic material at the top; A is a mineral layer at or near the surface where organic matter has been worked into the mineral grains; B is a mineral layer that formed below A and shows changes such as new structure or clay and iron brought down from above; C is unconsolidated mineral material with little or no soil formation in it. Horizons are roughly parallel to the surface and form in place as water, roots and animals work on the parent material. Their thickness varies from place to place; the depths drawn here (O about 3 cm, A to about 25 cm, B to about 80 cm) are typical values for a lawn soil, not measured at this spot. Darwin measured the dark mould that earthworms work as usually 4 or 5 to 10 and even 12 inches thick (about 10 to 30 cm), which is the range of the topsoil drawn here.
layers.expert: Different classification systems (the World Reference Base, FAO, the US Soil Taxonomy) use the same master letters with different definitions, so horizon names are not interchangeable between them. Many soils have extra horizons: E, a pale layer from which clay and iron have been washed out, sits between A and B in some acid soils; R is hard rock. The profile drawn here is a simplified typical one for a lawn on sandy and pebbly parent material, not a described profile from a survey. On acid sandy parent material the pale E layer is common and humus and iron are washed down into the B layer: soils on Blackheath Beds south of London are mapped as humo-ferric podzols of this kind (LandIS). A clay-enriched B layer, as in many loams, would be less expected here. The wavy boundaries between the horizons are drawn to look natural, not measured.

facts: organic: litter and thatch (drawn about 3 cm)
topsoil: mineral grains with organic matter (to about 25 cm)
subsoil: changed by weathering and by material moved down (to about 80 cm)

title: O horizon: litter and thatch
summary: The O horizon is the thin top layer of a soil made of dead plant material: leaf litter and the matted dead grass and roots of the lawn.

layers.basics: On the lawn this layer is only a few centimetres thick: the felt of old grass stems and roots (called thatch) and, near the oak, a scatter of fallen leaves. It is the soil's larder and its first stage of recycling. Fungal threads grow through it, and woodlice, springtails and mites eat their way through it. Below it, the dark topsoil begins.
layers.deeper: The O horizon holds organic material that is only partly decayed; in some descriptions a 'litter layer' is the part where more than 90 % of the volume is still recognisable dead plant tissue. Much of what lies at the top of a lawn is thatch: grass leaves, stems and roots that die faster than they decompose. Darwin watched earthworms drag leaves into their burrows, which is one way plant remains are carried from the surface into the soil.
layers.expert: The O horizon is drawn 3 cm thick, a model choice. The litter on the surface (oak leaves about 10 cm long, tilted into the grass) shows how the layer is fed from above. Fungal threads in the layer are drawn about 40 times too thick; real hyphae are 4 to 6 micrometres across. In Whole profile cut the layer shows a dark pattern; its colours, like all the cut-face colours, are a code.

facts: dead plant material: litter, thatch, dead roots
woodlice, springtails, mites, earthworms, fungi, bacteria

title: A horizon: the topsoil
summary: The A horizon is the topsoil: mineral grains mixed with dark, decayed organic matter, where most roots, fungi and soil animals live.

layers.basics: This is the layer you would call 'the soil' in a garden. It is dark because decayed plant material (humus) has been mixed into the mineral grains, mostly by earthworms and other animals. It is crumbly: the grains are stuck into little lumps called crumbs, with pores between them for air and water. Grass roots and the oak's fine roots spread through it, and most of the animals in this block live in it. In the model it reaches to about 25 cm.
layers.deeper: Because organic matter, roots and animals are concentrated here, the A horizon is the most biologically active part of the profile. Darwin found that the dark vegetable mould of old pasture was usually 4 or 5 to 10, and even 12, inches thick, and that earthworms pass it over and over through their bodies. In the block the topsoil shows the pocket of crumbs and pores on the cut face, flint pebbles, fungal threads and fine roots with their fungal sleeves, and the burrow of the earthworm.
layers.expert: The boundary with the O horizon above is drawn at 3 cm and with the B horizon below at about 25 cm, with a gentle undulation; both depths are typical values, not measured. The pocket of crumbs (4 to 9 mm across) is drawn on a patch of the face about 36 cm wide; in real topsoil crumb structure continues through the layer, and crumb size and stability depend on the soil.

facts: worm-worked mould usually 4 or 5 to 10 or 12 inches thick (≈ 10 to 30 cm)

title: B horizon: the subsoil
summary: The B horizon is the subsoil: a paler, firmer layer below the topsoil that weathering has changed. In many soils it collects clay or iron washed down from above; on acid sandy gravels it is more likely to be sandy.

layers.basics: Under the dark topsoil the soil turns paler and yellower-brown. There is much less dead plant matter here, fewer roots and far fewer animals. In many soils this is the zone where water seeping down leaves behind fine clay particles and iron compounds. The block is drawn as a typical lawn soil, so it includes a little clay here; the soils on the Blackheath sands and gravels are probably sandier. In the block, a thick oak root crosses this layer and its cross-section shows in the cut. Click the clay hotspot to look at a single clay particle.
layers.deeper: The B horizon forms below the A horizon and shows soil-forming changes: new structure, new clay formed by weathering, or material moved down from above (a process called illuviation). On very acid sandy material the moved material is mostly humus and iron rather than clay, giving a podzol; the soil association that LandIS maps over the Blackheath and Woolwich Beds south of London is dominated by such humo-ferric podzols. A few earthworm burrows from the deep-burrowing species go through the B horizon and let roots follow them down.
layers.expert: The B horizon is drawn between about 25 and 80 cm, a typical depth, not a measured one. No soil survey of Greenwich Park itself was found, so whether the soil at any spot is podzolic, a brown earth or something disturbed by park use is not known; the horizon is drawn as a generic subsoil. Texture and colour depend on the exact site.

title: C horizon: the pebble bed the soil grew from
summary: The C horizon is the loose rock that a soil forms in. Here it is drawn as the Blackheath pebble bed: pale sand with many rounded flint pebbles.

layers.basics: At the bottom of the block lies the material the soil above has been made from. It is almost unchanged: no dark organic matter, few roots, no animals. Under Greenwich Park's high plateau this material is sand with many rounded black pebbles, all of them flint. The pebbles do not weather quickly, so they stay behind as the sand around them becomes soil, and some of them reach the surface.
layers.deeper: In soil science, C is unconsolidated mineral material (you could dig it with a spade) in which soil formation has had little effect. Beneath it, the geological column continues, here for several metres, as the next card describes. The pebbles in this layer are drawn 2.4 to 7 cm across; their number is illustrative.
layers.expert: The block ends at 1.2 m, well inside a bed that the geological survey puts at up to 10 m thick at the top of the park, so the real C horizon continues far below the bottom of the block. The pebble sizes and number are model choices; what is sourced is that the pebbles are rounded flint and that the sand and gravel are what lies below the plateau.

facts: Blackheath pebble bed: sand and rounded flint pebbles

title: What lies under Greenwich Park
summary: The high plateau of Greenwich Park stands on the Blackheath pebble beds, a gravel and sand formed in a shallow sea about 55 million years ago, and below it lie clays and sands, then Thanet Sand and Chalk.

layers.basics: Greenwich Park is a hill: its steep slope falls about 25 metres to the River Thames, and the flat top, the Blackheath plateau, is made of sand and gravel. The pebbles in the gravel are rounded black flints, which started as layers in the Chalk, were washed out and rolled for a long time, probably by the sea, and were laid down again. Water falling on the plateau soaks down through the gravel and sand until it meets clay about 15 metres below the top of the slope, and comes out as springs. The block you see is a very thin slice of the top of that story: soil on the sand and pebbles.
layers.deeper: From the top down, as the London Geodiversity Partnership's geotrail describes it: the Blackheath pebble beds (the Blackheath Member of the Harwich Formation), up to about 10 m thick on Blackheath and at the top of the park; then the sands and clays of the Lambeth Group (including the Woolwich and Reading formations and, at the base, the Upnor Formation sand); then the Thanet Sand; then the Chalk. A spring line appears where the permeable gravel meets clay. The Harwich Formation dates from about 55 million years ago, and the Blackheath pebbles were laid down under the sea. The top surface of the pebble bed is at much the same height, 40 to 45 m, from Blackheath to Erith, 13 km away.
layers.expert: Younger deposits lie elsewhere: the Thames flood plain at the foot of the hill is alluvium (clays, sands and pebbles deposited in the last 10,000 years) and the Kempton Park Gravel, a Thames terrace laid down 100,000 to 50,000 years ago, is near the surface a few steps from the river. The block shows only the soil on the plateau's pebble bed. The geotrail does not describe the soil itself; the soil layers in the block and their depths are typical for a lawn soil on sand and gravel, not read from a survey of the park. The park register describes the southern half as high gravel plateau and the northern part as low-lying flood plain, separated by a ridge about 25 m high. Chalk lies deep below the park (it was mined nearby, in caverns at Blackheath), and at 1.2 m the block is nowhere near it.

title: Lawn grass and its root mat
summary: A lawn is a dense mat of grass leaves above and a felt of fine roots and dead stems below, which holds the soil together and feeds the layers underneath.

layers.basics: The lawn here is drawn 4 centimetres tall, and what you see is only the upper part of each plant. Each plant is a tuft of narrow leaves that grow from the base, so mowing does not kill them. Below the surface the same plants have a dense mass of fine roots in the top layer of soil. Together, the leaves and the root mat form the turf. The roots hold the soil, the dead leaves and roots become the thatch, and each time the grass is cut the clippings add dead plant matter that decomposers recycle. In the model, one patch of lawn covers the top of the block and sways a little in a drawn breeze.
layers.deeper: Grasses are flowering plants whose leaves grow from the base, which is why they survive grazing and mowing. Their roots are fibrous: many fine roots rather than one tap root. A mat of such roots binds the soil particles; fine roots release sugars and other compounds that feed bacteria and fungi around them (the rhizosphere), and root and fungal products help stick mineral grains into crumbs. Like other plants, grass absorbs most of its water and nutrients through its fine roots and root hairs.
layers.expert: The block draws 5,000 blades, each 4 cm high, as five-triangle strips in tufts; the number is illustrative and real lawns have far more. The species mix is not modelled (a typical British lawn contains several grasses and often white clover, a nitrogen-fixing legume; see the nitrogen card). Cellulose, the main structural material of the blades, can be viewed as a molecule fragment (cellotriose).

title: Leaf litter
summary: Fallen oak leaves lying on the lawn edge: the first food of the soil's recycling system.

layers.basics: Each autumn an oak drops its leaves. They lie on the ground and are the raw material of the O horizon. Fungi and bacteria soften them, woodlice and springtails and mites chew them, and earthworms pull pieces down into their burrows and eat them. Over time the leaf is eaten, digested, mixed with mineral grains and turned into the dark organic matter of the topsoil. The leaf shown is about the size of a real oak leaf, 10 centimetres long.
layers.deeper: Leaf litter is mostly cellulose and lignin, the same materials as wood, plus smaller amounts of sugars, proteins and minerals. Soft parts go first; tough, lignin-rich parts last. Decomposition is the work of many organisms in sequence, not of one. Mixing litter into the mineral soil protects some of its carbon from further decay.
layers.expert: The oak leaf in the card is drawn from a lobed outline 8 to 12 cm long (the oak card gives 10 to 12 cm); 46 leaves are scattered with a lean to the oak side. How fast a leaf disappears depends on climate, the leaf and the animals present; the model gives no rate. Cellulose can be viewed as a molecule.

facts: 8 to 12 cm (oak leaves are 10 to 12 cm)
fungi, bacteria, woodlice, springtails, mites, earthworms

title: Flint pebbles
summary: Flint pebbles are the rounded, dark, extremely hard stones in the Blackheath pebble bed: lumps of quartz that formed in chalk and were rolled smooth.

layers.basics: The stones in this block are flints. Flint is a very hard stone made of quartz (silica) in crystals so small you cannot see them, which formed as lumps inside the Chalk, long before the sand above it. When the Chalk wore away, the flints were washed out and tumbled until they were rounded, and were laid down again in the Blackheath pebble bed. Break one and the edge is sharp, which is why flint was used for tools. In the block they are thickest in the bottom layer; a few have worked up into the soil and one or two lie on the lawn.
layers.deeper: Flint is a cryptocrystalline form of quartz (silicon dioxide, SiO2), found chiefly as nodules in chalk and limestone, with a dark grey or black interior and usually a white rough rind. The geotrail says the Blackheath pebbles are all flint that originated as layers within the White Chalk, that they were rounded by long transport, probably by the sea, and that the size of the pebbles implies deposition by high-energy currents. Because flint is so resistant to weathering, it stays as the softer minerals around it break down. Quartz can be viewed as a crystal.
layers.expert: Pebble sizes in the block (2.4 to 7 cm) and their number are model choices; what is known is that the pebbles are rounded flint. In the cut, each pebble shows a dark cross-section. The quartz crystal you can open from this card is a lattice of alpha quartz, the mineral flint is made of, not the microcrystalline texture of flint itself.

facts: rounded by transport; sizes in the block 2.4 to 7 cm (model)

title: How soil forms, and how long it takes
summary: Soil forms slowly, as rock breaks down and living things add organic matter. Where it has been measured, the fastest rates of turning rock into soil range from about 0.05 to 2 millimetres a year, so a few centimetres take centuries.

layers.basics: Soil is made from rock by weathering: rain, frost and chemistry break rock into smaller pieces, and plants, fungi, bacteria and animals mix in dead matter. Time matters most. It takes decades to several thousand years for a soil to develop a profile with layers. Where rates have been measured they are small: at some sites around a tenth of a millimetre of rock becomes soil each year, so a centimetre of soil can take about a hundred years. Earthworms speed up the mixing in a different way: Darwin buried chalk on a field and found it seven inches deep 29 years later, because worm casts piled up on top of it.
layers.deeper: Five things shape a soil, the classical factors named by Jenny in 1941: the parent material, the climate, the topography, the organisms and the time. Rates of soil production depend on how thick the soil already is: the soil production function says the rate falls roughly exponentially as the soil thickens, from a maximum P0 that was reported to range from 0.08 to 2.0 mm a year for sites in northern California and 0.05 to 0.14 mm a year for sites in south-east Australia. In Sicily a production rate of approximately one tenth of a millimetre a year was reported. These are rates of turning rock into soil, a different process from the burial of objects by worm casts, and they say nothing about this particular block.
layers.expert: No measured rate of soil formation for Greenwich Park is used here. Chemical weathering roughly doubles for each 10 degrees C rise in temperature but depends strongly on water. At 0.1 mm a year, 10 mm of soil takes 100 years, and a soil 25 cm deep would need about 2,500 years. The topsoil of old pasture can also thicken from above, because earthworms bring fine earth up: Darwin's measurement is on the Darwin card. The rates quoted here are summaries of published field studies at particular sites; they are not typical of every soil.

title: Soil crumbs (aggregates)
summary: Soil crumbs are small lumps in which mineral grains, humus, roots and fungal threads are stuck together; the gaps between crumbs are the soil's pores.

layers.basics: Rub a handful of good topsoil between your fingers and it falls apart into crumbs. Each crumb is a lump of sand, silt and clay grains glued together with sticky decayed plant matter, clay, fine roots and the threads of fungi. Between the crumbs are gaps (pores) that hold air and water. A soil made of crumbs is easy for roots to push through, drains well and still holds water; a soil with no crumbs sets hard like a brick when dry. Click the patch of crumbs on the cut face of the topsoil to see the pores, or look inside a crumb to see what it is made of.
layers.deeper: Soil particles are bonded into aggregates (peds) by iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus. In the topsoil, biological products matter as much: fungal hyphae, biofilms and glycoproteins help bind particles, and the breakdown products of organic matter both separate and bridge mineral particles. Earthworms improve soil structure where they were previously absent, as was seen in recent polders. A granular structure, roughly spherical or polyhedral lumps, allows good porosity and easy movement of air and water. Aggregate stability, the share of aggregates that do not fall apart in water, is used as an indicator of soil health.
layers.expert: In the block the crumbs are drawn as two layers of lumps, 4 to 9 mm across, in a patch about 36 cm by 14 cm of the A horizon face; their size and number are illustrative, and real soils have crumbs of many sizes at once, with smaller ones inside larger ones. The blue droplets at some contacts show water held in the narrowest gaps. The 'Look inside a soil crumb' scene shows one crumb at 2.2 mm field of view with the size classes of the grains, to scale.

title: Pores: what the space between the grains holds
summary: About half of a typical soil is empty space: pores that hold water and air, which roots, fungi and animals need.

layers.basics: Soil looks solid, but a typical soil is about half empty by volume. Those pores are as important as the grains. They are where the water is that roots drink, where the air is that roots, fungi, worms and bacteria breathe, and where small animals live and move. The pore space is shared between water and air, and the two trade places: after rain the pores fill with water and air is pushed out, and as the soil dries air moves back in. If soil is squashed (by footsteps or machines) the pores shrink, and air and water cannot get to the roots.
layers.deeper: A typical soil is about 50 % solids (about 45 % mineral and 5 % organic matter) and about 50 % voids; water and gas share the void space roughly equally on average, and the two vary inversely. Field capacity is the water remaining in soil two or three days after it has been thoroughly watered, with negligible free drainage; the permanent wilting point is the water content at which growing plants wilt and do not recover; the water between the two is the available water. The water that remains below the wilting point is held too tightly for plants to use. Coarse pores drain quickly; fine pores hold water.
layers.expert: In the model the pore space is the dark gap between the crumbs in the patch on the face of the topsoil. The proportions above are for a typical soil; real values depend on texture, structure and compaction, and a silt loam used as the worked example holds about 25 % water and 25 % gas by volume at the moment given. Carbon dioxide made by roots and organisms collects in the soil air; its molecule can be viewed from the pore-space scene of the crumb.

title: Water held in the pores
summary: Water clings to the grain surfaces and sits in the narrow gaps between crumbs; this is the water that plant roots drink.

layers.basics: After rain, water sinks down through the biggest pores. The water that stays behind sticks to the grains and gathers in the narrowest spaces, like the small droplets drawn here where crumbs touch. Roots and fungi take it up, with the dissolved minerals in it. Water is also how nutrients reach roots: they are dissolved in this thin film.
layers.deeper: The water that is left in a soil two or three days after a thorough wetting is called field capacity; plants can use water between that and the wilting point, but not the water below it, which is held too strongly. Water is the solvent that carries dissolved ions such as ammonium and nitrate to roots and away down the profile. Soil water is a very dilute solution, not pure water.
layers.expert: The blue droplets at about 15 % of the crumb contacts are a drawing of where water would collect, not a measurement; the size (about 1 to 3 mm across) and number are illustrative. A water molecule can be viewed from the card.

facts: attraction to grain surfaces and in narrow gaps

title: Oak roots (the thick ones)
summary: A thick oak root crosses the block: in the cut its cross-section shows as a tan disc about 2 cm across, and thinner roots branch from it.

layers.basics: The oak that stands a few metres away sends its roots out far beyond the shade of its crown. The thick roots hold the tree up and carry water and food; the thin ones branching from them do most of the drinking. In the cut face you can see one thick root cut across (a round disc) and others running along the face. Most of the roots in a block like this lie in the upper layers, where the water, air and nutrients are. Look inside the root wood to see what it is made of.
layers.deeper: Big roots store sugars and anchor the tree; finer roots take up water and minerals. Many trees put most of their roots in the upper layers of soil, though the pattern varies with soil and species. Root systems draw their shape from the soil: roots go where the water and nutrients are. The existing oak cards describe the whole tree and its roots; this block shows a small part of the system at true size.
layers.expert: The thick roots are drawn 2.2 cm across where cut, tapering to about 1.5 mm; their paths and the number of branches are drawn for illustration, not mapped from a real tree. The 'wood' scene shows the wood of an oak trunk (vessels about 0.5 mm wide, from the species description); root wood has the same kinds of cells but different proportions, which the scene does not distinguish.

facts: 2.2 cm across at the cut, tapering
anchors the tree, stores sugar, carries water

title: Oak fine roots
summary: Fine roots, less than a millimetre or two across, are the oak's working surface: they take up water and minerals and are replaced all the time.

layers.basics: Most of what the oak drinks comes through roots as fine as thread. They are short-lived and are replaced all the time. In this block hundreds of them run through the topsoil, thickest near the surface and thinning with depth. Many of their tips are covered by a fungus that works with the tree (the pale sleeves). Bare tips carry root hairs, which are too small to draw in the block; look at the tip of one fine root, wrapped in its fungus, close up in the scene.
layers.deeper: Roots take up water by osmosis and ions by transporters, mostly near the tips where root hairs form. Root hairs are outgrowths of single epidermal cells, 15 to 17 micrometres wide and 80 to 1,500 micrometres long in published values for root hairs in general. Oak's fine root tips are usually covered by fungus and so have few or no root hairs, which is why the model shows both kinds of tip separately.
layers.expert: In the block each fine root is a tapering axis about 4 cm long and 1.1 mm across at its base, with nine short tapering side roots; the shapes and the number (about 640 axes) are illustrative and far fewer than real topsoil holds. Root hairs are not drawn in the block, because at 15 to 17 micrometres wide they are far thinner than anything at this scale. The close-up scene (2.6 mm field of view) shows a sheathed tip: its sleeve is drawn at the 40 micrometre upper limit from the published range, but the tip's own length and width are illustrative.

facts: 15 to 17 µm wide, 80 to 1,500 µm long (published, general)

title: Root tips wrapped in fungus (ectomycorrhiza)
summary: Many of the oak's finest root tips are wrapped in a sleeve of fungus; the fungus carries water and minerals to the tree and receives sugar from it.

layers.basics: The pale, slightly swollen tips drawn here are not bare roots: each is an oak root tip inside a fungal sleeve. The fungus grows white threads out into the soil, far beyond what the root could reach. In return the tree gives the fungus sugar from its leaves. This partnership is called ectomycorrhiza ('fungus outside the root cells'); some of the mushrooms you find under oaks in autumn are the fruiting bodies of such fungi. Look inside one to see the sleeve and the threads between the root's cells.
layers.deeper: The fungus forms a mantle around the root tip, which can be up to 40 micrometres thick, and grows between the root cells without entering them in a network called the Hartig net, where nutrients and sugars change hands. Hyphae extending from the mantle into the soil gather water and minerals, singly or in aggregated strands called rhizomorphs. Ectomycorrhiza forms on the roots of about 2 % of plant species, including the beech family, to which oaks belong. The tree gives sugar made in its leaves and the fungus gives mostly nitrogen and phosphorus. The existing oak mycorrhiza card covers the evidence on shared 'networks' between trees, which is contested.
layers.expert: The tips are drawn 1.2 mm across and 4.7 mm long, which is a model choice; the scene (0.7 mm field of view) shows a root tip with its mantle and Hartig net, with the thread width at the real 5 micrometres (range 2 to 10) and everything else illustrative.

title: Fungal threads in the soil (hyphae)
summary: Fungi live in soil as a web of microscopic threads that digest dead plant matter, bind the crumbs, and carry water and minerals.

layers.basics: Most of a soil fungus is hidden: a web of threads, each far thinner than a hair, growing through the litter and the soil. The threads digest dead leaves from outside, absorb the food, and hold the soil together. Some partner with roots (the tips on the oak). They are the 'rotting' in decay and, together with bacteria, the main recyclers in the soil. The threads in the block are drawn about 40 times thicker than real ones so that you can see them. Click the hotspot near the litter, or a root tip, to see a thread at its real size in a scene.
layers.deeper: A hypha is a tube 2 to 10 micrometres wide (about 4 to 6 in many fungi) that grows at its tip. Fungi release enzymes into the litter and take up the products; they are major decomposers, and springtails feed on their threads and spores. Fungal threads and their sticky products help stick mineral particles into crumbs. A gram of garden soil can contain around a million fungi.
layers.expert: The drawn threads are 0.2 mm wide and 5 cm long, in a cloud of about 500 through the litter and the top 16 cm of topsoil, which is an illustration, not a measure of how much fungus a real soil holds. The fungal species are not identified.

facts: digests dead matter, binds crumbs, partners with roots

title: Decomposition: who eats a dead leaf
summary: A dead leaf is recycled by a relay of animals, fungi and bacteria: the animals shred it, the fungi and bacteria digest it, and carbon dioxide, mineral nutrients and humus come out.

layers.basics: When a leaf falls it is not simply 'rotting'. First woodlice, springtails, mites and earthworms bite it into smaller pieces and pull some of it into the soil. Fungi and bacteria then digest those pieces from outside, using enzymes. Tiny nematodes and other animals graze on the bacteria and fungi. At the end, the carbon from the leaf has gone back to the air as carbon dioxide (breathed out by all these organisms), the nutrients are back in the soil water where roots can take them up, and a dark remnant called humus is left in the soil. Without this recycling the forest floor would be buried in its own dead leaves.
layers.deeper: Different organisms do different jobs. Woodlice are detritivores that fragment plant matter without grinding it finely, so they contribute little to mineralisation themselves; oribatid mites help break down detritus and distribute fungi; springtails commonly eat fungal threads and spores; nematodes graze on bacteria and fungi; earthworms swallow soil and litter and grind it in a gizzard. Fungi and bacteria do most of the chemical breakdown. The decomposers are respiring: the carbon in leaf sugars and cellulose goes back to the air as carbon dioxide.
layers.expert: The speed of decomposition depends on temperature, moisture, the leaf and the community; the relay is simplified (real food webs are far more tangled). The cards for each animal give the facts and sources.

title: Carbon in the soil, in the air and in plants
summary: The world's soils and litter hold about 1,500 to 2,400 petagrams of carbon, roughly two to three times as much as the whole atmosphere, and more than the living plants.

layers.basics: Plants take carbon dioxide from the air and build their bodies from it. When plants and animals die, much of that carbon goes into the soil as dead roots, leaves and the dark organic matter humus. Across the Earth, soil and litter hold roughly twice to three times as much carbon as is in the whole atmosphere, and more than the living plants do. That is why the soil under your feet matters for the climate: a small change in how much carbon soils hold is a large change compared with what is in the air. The soil in this block is a very small piece of that store.
layers.deeper: The IPCC Fifth Assessment Report gives these reservoir sizes in petagrams of carbon (1 PgC = 10^15 g = a thousand million tonnes): the atmosphere, 828 PgC (at a carbon dioxide level of about 390.5 parts per million in 2011); living plants (vegetation), 450 to 650 PgC; dead organic matter in litter and soils, 1,500 to 2,400 PgC. There is additional old soil carbon in wetland soils (300 to 700 PgC) and in permafrost soils (about 1,700 PgC), with some overlap with the other numbers. Plants take about 123 ± 8 PgC a year out of the air by photosynthesis; plant, microbial and animal respiration puts carbon back. Dividing the ranges, 1,500 and 2,400 by 828, puts litter and soils at about 1.8 to 2.9 times the carbon in the atmosphere.
layers.expert: The ranges are wide because soil carbon is hard to measure: it varies from place to place and with depth, and surveys differ in how deep they count. The 1,500 to 2,400 PgC figure is traced in the report to a 1996 compilation (Batjes) and the plant figure to Prentice and colleagues (2001). How long carbon stays in the soil depends on the soil and the climate; whether warming will speed decomposition and release more of it is an active research question. The block holds a vanishingly small share of the total.

open_questions: How much of the carbon in soils will be released as the climate warms, and how fast, is still being studied.

title: Nitrogen in the soil: fixation, recycling and uptake
summary: Plants need nitrogen, but the air's nitrogen gas is useless to them until microbes change it: in soil, fixation, ammonification, nitrification and uptake form a cycle driven mostly by microbes.

layers.basics: Four-fifths of the air is nitrogen gas, but plants cannot use it. A few kinds of bacteria can turn it into ammonia, a process called nitrogen fixation: some live free in the soil, and some live in swellings (nodules) on the roots of clover and other legumes. Other microbes break down dead plant and animal matter and release ammonium. Others change ammonium to nitrate, which roots take up easily and which can be washed away. The oak in the block gets part of its nitrogen through its fungal partners. Earthworm casts are richer in nitrogen than the soil around them.
layers.deeper: Soil steps, as the standard accounts describe them. Fixation: nitrogenase, the enzyme complex that reduces nitrogen gas (N2) to ammonia (NH3), is found in free-living bacteria such as Azotobacter and in rhizobia living in legume root nodules, and it is damaged by oxygen. The overall reaction, N2 + 16 ATP + 16 H2O + 8 e- + 8 H+ gives 2 NH3 + H2 + 16 ADP + 16 Pi, is costly in energy. Ammonification: bacteria and fungi convert organic nitrogen into ammonia and ammonium. Nitrification, oxidising ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate: the textbook account names Nitrosomonas for the first step and Nitrobacter for the second, but in soils the ammonia-oxidisers include archaea as well as bacteria (in a survey of 12 soils, archaeal amoA genes were up to 3,000 times more abundant than bacterial ones), and since 2015 some Nitrospira bacteria have been shown to do both steps in one cell (complete ammonia oxidisers, or comammox). Which group does most of the work varies with the soil, so Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are examples, not the whole story. Denitrification: bacteria such as Pseudomonas reduce nitrate back to nitrogen gas without oxygen. Assimilation: plants absorb nitrate or ammonium through their roots. Nitrate is very soluble and soils hold anions poorly, so it can leach into groundwater. About 30 % of total fixed nitrogen is made industrially by the Haber-Bosch process.
layers.expert: Darwin quoted analyses by Dr Gilbert of earthworm castings from a lawn: 0.35 (per cent) nitrogen, two to three times as much as ordinary arable surface soil. This block does not model nodules or nitrifying microbes as parts: the bacteria in the crumb scene are not identified by species, and the nitrogen-fixing legumes of the lawn are not drawn. Ammonium and nitrate are available as molecules from the soil scenes, and clay particles can hold ammonium as one of their exchangeable cations. How the ammonia-oxidising archaea, bacteria and comammox share the work in a particular soil is an area of active research.

open_questions: How much of soil nitrification is done by ammonia-oxidising archaea, by ammonia-oxidising bacteria and by comammox bacteria, and how that depends on acidity and fertiliser, is still being worked out.

title: How many organisms live in a handful of soil?
summary: A handful of soil holds billions of microbes and, depending on where it is, hundreds of larger animals; the numbers are estimates, and they vary widely from place to place.

layers.basics: There is no single answer, because soils differ so much, but every estimate is enormous. In one gram of soil (a pinch) there are of the order of a hundred million bacteria, and in a teaspoon of productive soil between a hundred million and three billion. Fungi: around a million per gram of garden soil. Larger animals are fewer but still many: a square metre of farm pasture in the UK has been found to hold hundreds of earthworms in its top 10 centimetres, against only 13 in one garden counted in Darwin's day. Soil is also home to more kinds of life than any other habitat: one recent review estimates that about 59 per cent of all species live in soil, with a spread of plus or minus 15 per cent.
layers.deeper: Sizes, from the soil biology classification: macrofauna 2 to 20 mm (earthworms, woodlice, ants), mesofauna 100 micrometres to 2 mm (mites, springtails, small worms), and microfauna and microflora 1 to 100 micrometres (protozoa, nematodes, bacteria and fungi). The numbers: mean prokaryote density roughly 10^8 per gram of soil; bacteria 100 million to 3 billion in a teaspoon of productive soil; fungi about 10^6 per gram of garden soil; nematodes often more than a million per square metre, about 90 % of them in the top 15 cm; springtails up to about 100,000 per square metre in some estimates. Earthworms, two counts a century and a half apart: Hensen's garden count quoted by Darwin, 53,767 per acre, which is 13 per square metre; and a modern survey of 28 pasture fields on UK farms (Hodson and colleagues 2021), whose totals of 13,298 worms from about 530 pits of 20 by 20 centimetres, dug to 10 centimetres, work out at roughly 25 worms per pit, about 600 per square metre. A pilot survey of English farms (Stroud 2019) quotes 150 to 350 per square metre as typical for arable soils and 400 or more as high. Methods, depth and season differ, so these are not a trend.
layers.expert: Counting soil life is hard: most microbes cannot be grown in a dish and are counted by chemical methods, and animals are extracted or dug and sorted by hand, so every figure is an estimate with a method behind it. The 59 ± 15 % figure for the share of species in soil comes from Anthony and colleagues (PNAS 2023), who reviewed the biodiversity literature. It is the average of their low, middle and high estimates, with the spread among those three, and it leaves out phages (viruses of bacteria); including the very numerous phages brings the soil share down to about 21 ± 11 %. The total number of species on Earth, soil or not, is itself uncertain by orders of magnitude.

title: Clay: the finest particles
summary: Clay particles are the smallest mineral grains in soil, less than two thousandths of a millimetre across, flat plates with electrically charged surfaces that hold water and nutrients.

layers.basics: Soil grains come in three size groups. Sand is the biggest, silt is in between, and clay is the smallest: under 2 micrometres, too small to see even with a good lens. Clay particles are not tiny bits of ordinary rock: they are flat plates made of layers of silicon, aluminium and oxygen. Their flat surfaces carry electric charge, which lets them hold on to nutrient ions such as potassium and ammonium. Look at clay plates, drawn here 1.4 to 1.8 micrometres wide, inside the clay size range, with the ions they hold.
layers.deeper: On the ISO scale used here, sand is 63 micrometres to 2 mm, silt 2 to 63 micrometres, and clay below 2 micrometres (some classification systems put the clay limit at 4 micrometres). Clay minerals are layered phyllosilicates built of sheets of silica tetrahedra and alumina octahedra; kaolinite, a 1:1 clay, forms pseudohexagonal plates, and its layers are uncharged and held together by hydrogen bonds. 2:1 clays carry a net negative charge on their layers, which attracts cations; the interlayer space of smectite can also hold water.
layers.expert: How much clay the soil of the Greenwich plateau has at any particular place is not known: the clay in the B horizon is drawn as a typical presence, and soils on sandy gravels usually hold less clay than a loam.

facts: negative on many clays (2:1) and at edges; kaolinite layers are uncharged

title: Cation exchange: how clay holds nutrients
summary: Clay and humus carry negative charges that hold positively charged nutrient ions (calcium, potassium, magnesium, ammonium) and exchange them with the soil water, which keeps nutrients from washing away.

layers.basics: Many nutrients are dissolved as ions: atoms or small molecules with an electric charge. Calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium carry a positive charge. The surfaces of clay and humus carry negative charge, so these positive ions stick to them like iron filings to magnets, and are held there instead of draining away with the rain. The amount of positive charge a soil can hold is called its cation-exchange capacity, and it is why a clay or humus-rich soil is fertile for longer than a sandy one. Nitrate, which is negative, is not held, and can be washed away.
layers.deeper: Cation-exchange capacity (CEC) counts charge, not ions: it is reported in centimoles of charge per kilogram (older texts use milliequivalents per 100 g, which is the same number). A soil of 10 cmol/kg could hold 10 cmol of sodium but only 5 cmol of calcium, because calcium carries two charges. Negative charge comes from two sources: permanent charge, from substituting lower-charge elements for aluminium or silicon in the clay layers (it does not depend on pH), and variable charge, from hydroxyl groups on clay edges and from groups on organic matter, which lose protons at normal soil pH. The ions are held in a diffuse layer with their water shells and are easily replaced by others. Typical values in milliequivalents per 100 g: kaolinite 3, halloysite 12, illite 25, chlorite 40, smectite 85, vermiculite 150; humus 100 to 300.
layers.expert: The scene draws three clay plates 1.4 to 1.8 micrometres wide, inside the clay size range (the scale bar is 1 micrometre), with ions drawn about 200 times too large (a hydrated cation is a fraction of a nanometre across): the number and place of the ions are illustrative. Values differ between sources and even for one mineral (the table gives 3 for kaolinite, other sources give 1 to 15 or 3 to 15).

title: Common earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris)
summary: The common earthworm is a segmented animal that lives in a deep vertical burrow, comes to the surface to feed, and swallows soil and leaves; here it is drawn at true size with its insides.

layers.basics: This is the earthworm of lawns and gardens, also called the nightcrawler. A grown one is about 11 to 20 centimetres long, about the width of a pencil, and made of well over a hundred rings called segments. It has no eyes, no legs and no jaws. It lives in a permanent burrow that runs straight down into the subsoil, with a little heap of earth, a cast, at the entrance. It crawls up to pull leaves down and eat them, and swallows soil as it burrows. It breathes through its skin, which is why it needs moist soil. Click 'Open the earthworm' to see inside: a gut that runs from end to end, five pairs of hearts, a nerve cord, and two layers of muscle.
layers.deeper: Lumbricus terrestris is generally 110 to 200 millimetres long (90 to 300 mm when mature), 7 to 10 millimetres wide, with around 120 to 170 segments, often 135 to 150. It is an annelid, a segmented worm. The body is a tube within a tube: an outer body wall (cuticle and skin, circular muscle, longitudinal muscle) around a fluid-filled cavity, the coelom, which contains the gut, the blood vessels and the nerve cord. The fluid works as a hydrostatic skeleton. The animal is hermaphroditic but mates with another worm, and it normally and regularly mates at the surface. Natural lifespan is not known; some have lived six years in captivity. Earthworms make casts of mixed organic and mineral material on the surface, and Lumbricus makes permanent, deep, vertical burrows.
layers.expert: The model draws 150 segments, a 170 mm body of 8 mm diameter, a head lobe without eyes, a swollen clitellum toward the front, eight bristles on each segment but the first, a dorsal and a ventral blood vessel, five pairs of hearts, a ventral nerve cord with a swelling in each segment, and a gut with pharynx, oesophagus and its lime glands, crop, gizzard and intestine. Not drawn: the septa between segments, the typhlosole, the nephridia (excretory tubes), the reproductive organs, and the other blood vessels. The thickness of each body-wall layer is illustrative. The earthworm is a 170 mm adult drawn from typical measurements; every internal part is simplified and its positions along the body are approximate.

title: Earthworm: head lobe and mouth
summary: At the front of the earthworm is a small lobe over the mouth; the worm has no eyes, no teeth and no jaws, but the front end is its most sensitive part.

layers.basics: The front of the earthworm ends in a small rounded lobe that hangs over the mouth. The worm uses it to grip leaves and to feel its way. It has no eyes, but the front end is the most sensitive part of the body. It has no jaws or teeth of any kind; it pulls food in with its muscular pharynx and grinds it later inside.
layers.deeper: Darwin described the lobe (lip) as used for prehension, and the pharynx behind the mouth as pushed forward when the animal eats. The nerve ring around the pharynx, with the brain on top of it, lies just behind the lobe.
layers.expert: The lobe is drawn as an ellipsoid 5 mm wide, simplified; the first true segment, the peristomium, lies behind it. The head is where the worm's sensing is concentrated, and the brain lies just behind the lobe, above the pharynx.

title: Earthworm: body rings (segments) and skin
summary: The body is a row of about 150 nearly identical rings, or segments, covered with a thin moist skin through which the worm breathes.

layers.basics: Look closely and the worm is made of rings separated by shallow grooves. Each ring is a segment. A worm has the same number of segments all its life: it grows by making the segments larger, not by adding more. The skin is thin, covered with mucus and always moist; the worm breathes through it, so it cannot live in dry air, and it dries out and dies if it is left on dry pavement. Underneath the skin lie the layers of muscle. The rings go all the way along, from the head lobe to the tail point, which is why the animal is so flexible.
layers.deeper: A large worm has 100 to 200 almost cylindrical segments (Darwin), around 120 to 170 in Lumbricus terrestris (often 135 to 150). Respiration is cutaneous, through the moist skin and its capillaries. Earthworms have no means of limiting water loss; Lumbricus can tolerate a water loss of up to 70 % of its body weight. Most segments carry bristles and a pair of excretory tubes (nephridia).
layers.expert: Colours are a drawing choice: darker above, paler underneath. The body is drawn with a circular cross-section and gentle taper; the tail end is blunter in real worms and the cross-section can be flattened. There is no zoom-in scene for the skin.

title: Earthworm: the clitellum (the saddle)
summary: The clitellum is the swollen, paler band toward the front of an adult earthworm; it makes the cocoon in which the eggs are laid.

layers.basics: Adult earthworms have a smooth, thick band round the body toward the front: the saddle, or clitellum. It is seen only when the worm is sexually mature. Its colour varies from white to orange-red or reddish-brown, and a more orange or reddish saddle is a sign that the worm is ready to mate. Gland cells in the band make the cocoon, in which the eggs are stored. Worms are both male and female at once, but they still pair up with another worm and swap sperm.
layers.deeper: The clitellum is a glandular section of the body wall found in earthworms and leeches and gives the group its name, the clitellates. It secretes a viscous fluid that forms the cocoon (and in many earthworms an albumin that nourishes the eggs). Lumbricus mates at the surface. Which segments the clitellum covers differs between species and is used to tell them apart.

title: The earthworm burrow

layers.basics: Unlike garden worms that wander through the topsoil, this worm digs a permanent vertical tunnel and lives in it for years. It comes to the mouth at night, pulls in leaves and sometimes mates there. Burrows like this do three jobs: they let air into the soil, they let rainwater drain deep instead of running off, and they give roots an easy path down through hard soil. In the block the burrow goes straight down through every layer to about a metre.

title: Earthworm cast
summary: A cast is the small heap of fine earth that an earthworm leaves at the mouth of its burrow: soil that has passed through its gut.

layers.basics: The little heap of crumbly earth at the top of the burrow is the worm's waste: soil and leaf matter that went through its body. Darwin collected and weighed them. He found that a single full-sized cast at the mouth of a burrow often weighs more than an ounce (about 28 grams), and that over a year the worms on a field bring up several tons of earth per acre. Casts are richer in nitrogen than the soil around them and are a fine crumbly material, and rain slowly spreads them out.
layers.deeper: Casts are mixed organic and mineral material deposited on the soil surface. Darwin collected the castings from two square yards at Leith Hill Place, Surrey, for a year and calculated 7.56 and 16.1 tons per acre of dried earth (about 19 and 40 tonnes per hectare). A lawn analysed by Dr Gilbert gave castings with 0.35 (per cent) nitrogen, two to three times as much as ordinary arable surface soil.
layers.expert: The cast is drawn as a heap of 38 pellets 3 to 7 mm across at the mouth of the burrow. Darwin noted that the amount he collected was somewhat less than the worms had ejected, because rain washes away some of the finest earth.

title: Earthworm: circular muscle
summary: Just under the skin is a thin layer of muscle whose fibres run around the body like hoops; when it tightens, the segment gets thinner and longer.

layers.basics: The worm has two layers of muscle that work against each other. The outer, thin one runs around the body in rings. When a stretch of the body tightens these hoops, the fluid inside has nowhere to go but along the body, so that stretch becomes long and thin and pushes forward through the soil, much as a long water balloon gets longer and thinner when you squeeze a ring round it. The other layer, the longitudinal muscle, does the opposite.
layers.deeper: Each segment has a thin outer layer of circular muscle and a thicker inner layer of longitudinal muscle. The coelomic fluid acts as a hydrostatic skeleton: a fluid cannot be squeezed to a smaller volume, so when circular muscle narrows a segment it must lengthen. Waves of contraction travelling along the body alternately shorten and lengthen it, and shortened segments are anchored by the bristles.

title: Earthworm: longitudinal muscle
summary: Under the circular muscle is a thick layer of muscle running from head to tail; when it tightens, the segment gets shorter and fatter and grips the burrow.

layers.basics: The inner layer of muscle runs along the body, from head to tail, in several bundles. When a stretch of it tightens, that part of the worm shortens and bulges outward, pressing against the burrow wall and gripping it with the bristles. Shortened, fat stretches act as anchors, while the stretches ahead are pushed forward by the circular muscle. A wave of this, repeated along the body, is how the worm moves. A sharp touch sets off an escape reflex: giant nerve fibres run along the nerve cord and the body muscles twitch, pulling the worm back (see the nerve cord card).
layers.deeper: In fresh specimens the longitudinal muscle is white or grey and is not interrupted at the segment boundaries. The quick escape reflex when the worm is touched at either end is carried by giant nerve fibres in the ventral nerve cord, and ends in a sudden contraction of the body muscles (see the nerve cord card).
layers.expert: The layer is drawn between 0.24 and 0.66 mm below the surface; the thickness is illustrative. There is no zoom-in scene for the muscle.

facts: a touch at either end sets off giant nerve fibres and a quick contraction

title: Earthworm: the body cavity (coelom)
summary: Between the body wall and the gut is a cavity filled with fluid; the fluid is the worm's skeleton.

layers.basics: An earthworm has no bones. Its stiffness comes from a liquid-filled space running its whole length, the coelom, divided into compartments by thin walls between the segments. Because the liquid cannot be squashed, the muscles can use it like a hydraulic system: squeezing one end makes the other end stretch. This kind of skeleton is called a hydrostatic skeleton, and many soft animals use it.
layers.deeper: The coelomic fluid functions as the hydrostatic skeleton. The coelom is divided by septa between the segments. It is lined with a membrane (the peritoneum) on the inner surface of the body wall, and the nephridia open into it. In the model the cavity is drawn as a pale tube between the muscle and the gut.
layers.expert: The coelom is drawn as a solid pale shape for the cut face; in life it is fluid and contains the gut, vessels and nerve cord. The septa are not drawn.

facts: fluid; the gut, vessels and nerve cord run through it

title: Earthworm: pharynx
summary: The pharynx is a strong muscular pump behind the mouth that sucks in leaves and soil.

layers.basics: Behind the mouth is a thick, muscular bulb. When the worm eats, it pushes the bulb forward and pulls it back like a pump, drawing in bits of leaf and earth. It has no teeth; whatever it swallows goes on to be softened and ground inside.
layers.deeper: The pharynx has thick, muscular walls with radial muscles; the buccal cavity before it covers about the first three segments and the pharynx itself about segments 3 to 5. Darwin noted that the pharynx is pushed forward when the animal eats and compared it to the protrusible trunk of other annelids.
layers.expert: The pharynx is drawn as a bulb about 3.4 mm long and 3 mm wide, in the head end of the body; the nerve ring and brain lie around it.

title: Earthworm: oesophagus and its lime glands
summary: The oesophagus carries food back from the pharynx; on its sides are glands that make lime (calcium carbonate) and help the worm control calcium and acidity.

layers.basics: The gullet is a narrow tube about 8 millimetres long in the model. Along it are pouches and glands that put chalk (calcium carbonate) into the food. Darwin was struck by them: he found that nothing like them was known in any other animal, and discussed what they were for. The modern account is that they help the worm keep the level of calcium and the acidity of its blood in balance.
layers.deeper: In one anatomy text the oesophagus runs through segments 6 to 12; esophageal pouches lie around segments 10 to 11 and two pairs of calciferous glands lie behind them, just behind the fifth heart. Darwin described three pairs of large glands that secrete a surprising amount of carbonate of lime. They help to regulate calcium and pH.
layers.expert: The model draws two pairs of pouch-like glands, not three, as a simplification; descriptions of the number differ between Darwin (three pairs) and the modern anatomy text (two pairs of glands behind the pouches). Their position is approximate.

facts: calciferous (lime) glands; Darwin counted three pairs

title: Earthworm: crop

title: Earthworm: gizzard
summary: The gizzard is a tough muscular grinder lined with a hard membrane; the worm swallows grains of sand and small stones that work like millstones inside it.

layers.basics: Because the worm has no teeth, its food is ground inside. The gizzard has thick muscular walls and a hard lining, and it squeezes and grinds the food together with grains of sand and tiny stones that the worm has swallowed. Darwin found stones between about 1.3 and a little over 2.5 millimetres across in the gizzards and intestines of worms, and he thought they work like millstones.
layers.deeper: Darwin's description: the gizzard is lined with a smooth thick chitinous membrane and surrounded by weak longitudinal and powerful transverse muscles. Perrier saw these muscles in energetic action, so the grinding must be done chiefly by this organ. Grains of sand and small stones from 1/20 to a little more than 1/10 inch in diameter (1.3 to a little over 2.5 mm) are generally found in the gizzards and intestines. The gizzard opens into the intestine.
layers.expert: The gizzard is drawn as a barrel 4 mm long and 3.4 mm wide; its position is approximate. Modern anatomy texts call it the major site of mechanical digestion, where food is ground into smaller pieces, while Darwin's evidence for the grinding was the sand and stones he found in it and the strong muscles round it.

facts: thick, muscular, with a hard lining

title: Earthworm: intestine and the soil inside it
summary: The intestine runs straight from the gizzard to the vent at the tail; in it the ground food is digested and absorbed, leaving the cast.

layers.basics: Behind the gizzard the gut becomes a long, straight, thin-walled tube that runs almost to the tail. Here the food, which is mostly soil with bits of decayed leaf in it, is digested and the nutrients pass into the blood. A fold runs along the roof of the tube to give more surface to absorb through. What remains passes out at the tail end and is the cast. The dark filling in the model is the soil that is being digested.
layers.deeper: Darwin described the intestine as running in a straight course to the vent, with a remarkable structure, the typhlosole, a deep longitudinal involution of its walls that gives an extensive absorbent surface; the dorsal wall is invaginated in the intestine and the typhlosole is absent from the rectum. The earthworm swallows large amounts of soil; its casts are richer in nitrogen than the soil around them.
layers.expert: The typhlosole is not drawn; the intestine is shown as a simple tube 1.45 mm wide, with the soil inside drawn as an inner dark tube. The thickness of the wall is illustrative.

title: Earthworm: the blood vessels
summary: Two long blood vessels run the length of the gut, one above and one below, joined by the hearts; the blood is red because it carries haemoglobin.

layers.basics: The worm's blood travels in closed tubes. The big one above the gut, the dorsal vessel, carries blood forward toward the head; the big one below, the ventral vessel, carries it backward toward the tail. Short vessels in each segment link them. The blood carries oxygen picked up through the skin, in a red pigment (haemoglobin) dissolved directly in the blood and not packed in cells.
layers.deeper: There are five main closed vessels: dorsal, ventral, subneural and two lateroneural; each segment also has a pair of pallial vessels. Blood contains haemocytes and dissolved haemoglobin. In the dorsal vessel blood flows toward the head and in the ventral vessel toward the tail. Only the dorsal and ventral vessels are drawn.
layers.expert: The vessels are drawn 0.54 and 0.6 mm wide and in the same simple course from head to tail; their size is illustrative.

title: Earthworm: five pairs of hearts
summary: Five pairs of muscular loops, one pair in each of five segments just behind the head, ring the oesophagus and pump blood from the top vessel to the bottom one.

layers.basics: An earthworm has ten hearts: five pairs, in a row just behind the head. Each is a muscular loop that goes around the gullet and joins the vessel above the gut to the vessel below. Together they pump the blood. They are not like our heart: they are simple muscular tubes that squeeze.
layers.deeper: The hearts are a pair of aortic arches in segments seven through eleven, which ring the coelom and act as hearts; they are large, contractile, segmental blood vessels encircling the oesophagus. Blood is moved forward in the dorsal vessel and backward in the ventral.
layers.expert: The hearts are drawn as ten loops 0.5 mm thick around the oesophagus at segments 7 to 11. They are drawn at rest. The ATP button leads to the molecule that muscle cells use as fuel.

title: Earthworm: ventral nerve cord
summary: A solid nerve cord runs along the underside of the body, with a small cluster of nerve cells in each segment and giant fibres for a fast escape.

layers.basics: The worm's nervous system is a cord running along the belly, not the back as in us. In each segment (from about the fifth) the cord swells into a small knot of nerve cells that controls that ring and sends nerves to its muscles and skin. A few very thick nerve fibres run the whole length of the cord and carry the alarm signal very quickly, so that a touch can make the whole worm withdraw.
layers.deeper: The cord is double and solid, with a segmental ganglion in each segment from the fifth to the last and three pairs of segmental nerves from each ganglion. The giant axons: the medial giant fibre (about 0.07 mm across) carries signals from a touch at the front end toward the tail, and the lateral giant fibres (about 0.05 mm across, joined into one working unit) carry signals from the tail end toward the head; both end in a quick twitch of the body muscles, the escape reflex. In teaching-laboratory recordings from live worms at room temperature the medial fibre conducted at about 23 m/s (mean of one set of worms, spread 4.5) and about 30 m/s (another set), and the lateral fibres at about 8 m/s.
layers.expert: The cord is drawn as a tube 0.5 mm wide with a swelling per segment from the fifth; the giant axons are not drawn separately. The cord is on the underside (to the left in the sagittal view).

title: Earthworm: brain and nerve ring
summary: The earthworm's brain is a pair of small nerve-cell clusters on top of the pharynx, joined by two collars round it to a second cluster underneath.

layers.basics: A worm does not have much of a brain: a pair of tiny knots of nerve cells sits on top of the pharynx, and two nerve bands curve around the pharynx to join a second knot beneath it. From there the nerve cord runs down the belly.
layers.deeper: Paired cerebral ganglia (the brain) lie in segment 3, sub-pharyngeal ganglia in segment 4, joined by circum-pharyngeal connectives into a nerve ring. In earthworms the brain has moved back out of the very front of the animal into a more posterior segment, and the double ventral nerve cord has a pair of ganglia in each segment.
layers.expert: The model draws two ganglia 1 mm wide above the pharynx and a smaller one beneath it, joined by connectives round the pharynx. Their sizes are illustrative.

title: How an earthworm moves
summary: An earthworm crawls by waves of squeezing along its body: fat, short parts grip with their bristles while thin, long parts push ahead, so it can move through a tunnel exactly its own width.

layers.basics: Try to picture a tube full of water that you can squeeze with rings. Squeeze a ring and the water goes along the tube, making it longer and thinner ahead of it. Let go and the tube relaxes and shortens. A worm does this along its body in a wave from head to tail: stretches that are short and fat grip the walls with their bristles, stretches that are long and thin reach forward. It can crawl backwards as well as forwards, and Darwin noted that it can retreat into its burrow with extraordinary rapidity by the aid of its affixed tail. On smooth moist ground one was reported to move at about 20 metres per hour, which is about 5.6 millimetres per second.
layers.deeper: Peristalsis uses two sets of muscle in opposition against a fluid skeleton: contraction of the circular muscle lengthens and thins a segment, contraction of the longitudinal muscle shortens and fattens it. The shortened segments are anchored by their bristles. The speed given is a reported figure for surface movement on moist, flat terrain; it is not the speed of burrowing, which is slower and depends on the soil. Nocturnal forays at the surface were estimated to reach 19 m.
layers.expert: The worm in the block is drawn at rest, because the model cannot show a wave travelling along a body. The reported 20 m/h is a surface speed on moist, flat ground; burrowing through soil is slower and depends on the soil.

facts: ≈ 20 m/h (≈ 5.6 mm/s) on moist flat ground

title: Why earthworms matter: Darwin's measurements
summary: Charles Darwin measured how much earth worms bring up and found that in a few decades they bury objects on a field several inches deep.

layers.basics: In 1881 Darwin published a book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms, after years of watching them. He found that earthworms swallow soil below and leave it on the surface as casts, and that over the years this buries things. On a field of his near Down, he had spread chalk on the grass, and when he dug a trench 29 years later he found a line of chalk lumps 7 inches (18 cm) below the surface: the soil had risen at an average of 0.22 inch (5.6 mm) a year. He weighed casts collected for a year on two square yards at Leith Hill, Surrey, and calculated 7.56 and 16.1 tons of dry earth per acre per year. He concluded that it may be doubted whether there are many other animals which have played so important a part in the history of the world as these lowly organised creatures.
layers.deeper: How many worms? Darwin quoted Hensen's count of 53,767 worms to the acre (133,000 per hectare) in a garden (Hensen believed twice as many as in corn fields) and noted that worms in old pasture had not been counted. Taking 15 tons of casts per acre a year and half Hensen's number of worms, he calculated that each worm would eject about 20 ounces a year. Objects strewn on grass fields were buried 1.9 to 2.2 inches in 10 years in four fields (sandy, swampy and argillaceous pastures) and 0.83 inch in a poor one. He also estimated that worms live chiefly in the surface mould, usually 4 or 5 to 10 and even 12 inches thick, and from time to time burrow far deeper and bring up earth from below. Worms do not work in dry weather in summer, or in winter in severe frosts.
layers.expert: Darwin's figures are from a few English sites around 1870 and depend on the soil, the weather and the worm species present (he did not separate species); the density counts are from gardens. Modern work confirms that earthworms improve soil structure, for example in new polders where they had been absent. The sums above are Darwin's own; 7.56 and 16.1 long tons per acre are about 19 and 40 tonnes per hectare.

facts: 7 inches in 29 years (≈ 0.22 inch a year ≈ 5.6 mm a year)

title: Woodlouse (Oniscus asellus)
summary: The common woodlouse is not an insect but a land-living crustacean, a relative of crabs and shrimps; it eats dead plants and rotting wood.

layers.basics: Lift a flowerpot or a log and you will often find woodlice. A common woodlouse grows to about 16 millimetres long and 6 wide. It is flat, shiny brown-grey, made of overlapping plates, and has seven pairs of legs and two pairs of feelers (antennae); the second pair is long and the first so short that you can hardly see it. It is a crustacean, so closer to a crab than to a beetle; it breathes with modified limbs under its tail and loses water easily, which is why it gathers in damp places. It eats dead plant matter, especially partly decayed leaves, and also eats its own droppings to extract more from them. In this way it chews litter into small pieces for the fungi and bacteria that follow.
layers.deeper: Woodlice (Oniscidea) have a head, a pereon (thorax) of seven segments, each with a pair of legs, and a pleon (abdomen) of five segments plus a pleotelson. Some or all of the five pairs of pleopods are adapted for breathing. Woodlice are mainly detritivores that eat dead plant matter and reingest their faeces (coprophagy). Unlike earthworms, they fragment plant matter into small pieces without grinding it finely, so they contribute little to mineralisation; they are a major contributor to the humification process. They often gather under objects, which reduces moisture loss. Most woodlice cannot roll into a ball.
layers.expert: The model woodlouse is 15 mm long and 6.5 mm wide, with 13 body plates, two eyes, seven pairs of legs, long second antennae and two tail points (uropods); its plates are simplified and the short first antennae and the breathing structures under the tail are not drawn. Its chitin skeleton can be viewed as a molecule unit.

facts: dead plant matter; also its own droppings

title: Springtails (Collembola)
summary: Springtails are wingless, six-legged animals 1 to 2 millimetres long that live in huge numbers in leaf litter and soil, eating fungal threads and dead plant matter.

layers.basics: On the litter on the lawn, and in the crumbs of the topsoil, are specks the size of a full stop that jump when disturbed. They are springtails. A soil-living springtail is 1 to 2 millimetres long. Estimates of their numbers reach 100,000 in a square metre of ground. They live in leaf litter and rotting material and most eat fungal threads and spores as well as dead plant matter; a few eat other tiny animals. They are not insects: they belong to a separate group of six-legged animals, and there are more than 9,000 species. In the block there are about 16 of them in the litter and on the crumbs.
layers.deeper: Most springtails have a forked 'spring' (furcula) folded under the body and held under tension by a small catch (the retinaculum). When the catch lets go, the furcula snaps against the ground and flings the animal into the air; the whole action takes a few milliseconds. Many have a number of ocelli (simple eyes) from one to eight on each side of the head; blind species, mostly subterranean, lack them. They are free-living and moisture-loving. Springtails are normally under 6 mm long, and the species that live in the litter and the top of the soil are about 1 to 2 mm. Species that live deeper in the soil are often pale and blind and have a reduced or missing spring.
layers.expert: The model springtail is 1.8 mm long, a drawing of an elongated litter-dwelling species: body in 10 parts, four-segmented antennae drawn as bent tubes, six legs, and a folded spring. The block draws only this litter form. The pale, blind, small-spring or spring-less kinds that live deeper in the mineral soil (Wikipedia, Springtail: euedaphic species have a reduced or absent furca and lack pigment and ocelli) are not drawn. Eyes and the other details are not drawn. The spring is a separate part. The positions and the number (16) are illustrative.

facts: 1 to 2 mm for soil species (model: 1.8 mm)
furcula held by a catch; a jump takes a few milliseconds

title: Springtail: the spring (furcula)
summary: The spring is a forked tail-like limb folded under the springtail's body; it is held under tension and, when released, flings the animal into the air in a few milliseconds.

layers.basics: The reason springtails have their name is a small forked piece under the end of the body. It is held bent under the belly like a loaded spring. When the animal is startled, it lets go and the fork flicks against the ground, throwing the animal up and away faster than you can follow.
layers.deeper: The furcula is held under tension by the retinaculum (also called the tenaculum). When released, it snaps against the substrate and flings the animal into the air; the action takes a few milliseconds.
layers.expert: The model draws two short rods folded under the rear of the animal; real furcula have a base and two slender branches.

title: Oribatid mites (moss mites)
summary: Oribatid mites are tiny, hard-shelled, eight-legged soil animals, 0.2 to 1.4 millimetres long, that eat dead plant matter and fungi and help spread fungi through the soil.

layers.basics: On the leaf litter and between the crumbs live mites, relatives of spiders. The oribatid mites are the shiny, brown, dome-shaped ones, 0.2 to 1.4 millimetres long. Many of them have a hard, mineral-strengthened shell, like a tiny armoured beetle. They eat a wide variety of dead plant and fungal material, and help to break down dead matter and spread fungi. They develop slowly: from egg to adult may take from several months to two years in forest soil, and the adults live a relatively long time.
layers.deeper: Oribatida range from 0.2 to 1.4 mm. Many have a mineralised exoskeleton as adults, some with wing-like flaps (pteromorphae) over the legs, and some can tuck in their legs. They feed on living and dead plant and fungal material (non-parasitic ones; a few are predatory). Density is highest in forests with thick organic layers.
layers.expert: The model mite is 0.7 mm long, a dome with a small head and eight legs, with no further detail; 10 of them are placed on the litter and the crumbs, which is illustrative. Adult mites have eight legs, as arachnids do.

facts: several months to two years (forest soil)

title: Ground beetle (Pterostichus madidus)
summary: A black ground beetle 14 to 20 millimetres long, common in gardens and grassland, which hides under stones and in grass and is most often seen in summer.

layers.basics: This glossy black beetle is a common ground beetle of British gardens and grassland. It is usually 14 to 20 millimetres long, black with reddish-brown to black legs, and you will find it under stones, in grass or in loose bark. It is most abundant in summer and breeds in autumn. In Britain it is also called the rain beetle, because it tends to appear when rain is coming. It is mostly a predator of small animals on the ground, such as caterpillars and slugs, and also eats some plant matter. Click its head, its wing cases or its legs for the parts.
layers.deeper: The beetle's front wings are hardened into wing cases (elytra) that cover the folded flight wings and the abdomen; here the wing cases carry grooves running lengthwise. The skeleton is on the outside, made of chitin, which can be viewed as a molecule unit. The species is native to Europe.

Details such as the antennal joints and the leg spines are not drawn.
