title: Ground beetle: head, jaws and antennae
summary: The beetle's head has two large eyes, a pair of jaws that bite sideways, and two antennae for smell and touch.

layers.basics: The head carries two eyes, one on each side, two long feelers (antennae) that taste and smell the air and ground, and the jaws (mandibles), which open and close sideways like pincers.
layers.deeper: Beetle mouthparts are chewing mouthparts: the mandibles move sideways, not up and down, and the antennae carry the sense organs for smell and touch. The head is a rigid capsule of chitin.
layers.expert: The model head is 3.6 mm long with eyes, two curved jaws and two antennae; no mouthparts other than the jaws are drawn.

title: Ground beetle: legs

layers.basics: The beetle has six legs, three on each side, reddish-brown to black. It is found on the ground, under stones and in grass.
layers.deeper: Insects and other arthropods have jointed legs: the segments are joined by hinge joints and moved by muscles inside the hard skeleton.

title: Inside a soil crumb
summary: A window of about 2 millimetres into one soil crumb: sand grains, many smaller grains of silt, flakes of clay, dark humus, a film of water, air pores, bacteria, a nematode, a fungal thread and a root hair.

layers.basics: A crumb of topsoil looks like a brown lump, but under a microscope it is a crowded city. The big stones are sand grains. Between them are many smaller grains of silt and, smaller than anything you can see even in this view, flakes of clay. Everything is glued together by dark humus (decayed plant matter), fungal threads and bacterial slime. A thin film of water coats the grains, and the gaps that are not full of water are filled with air. Bacteria live on the film. A nematode, a microscopic worm, grazes on them. A root hair reaches in to drink. All are drawn at their own sizes against a scale bar. Click anything in the scene.
layers.deeper: The size classes are standard: sand grains 63 micrometres to 2 mm (fine 63 to 200, medium 200 to 630, coarse 630 to 2,000), silt 2 to 63 micrometres, clay below 2 micrometres. The sand of inland soils is mostly quartz, the most common mineral resistant to weathering. A bacterium is 0.5 to 5 micrometres long; a fungal thread 4 to 6 (2 to 10) micrometres wide; a root hair 15 to 17 micrometres wide and 80 to 1,500 long; free-living nematodes are often under 2.5 mm long, some about 1 mm. Aggregation is helped by humus, clay, iron oxides, fungal hyphae and biofilms.
layers.expert: Drawn to scale: the size classes of the mineral grains, the width of the bacteria, the thread and the root hair. Illustrative: the number and places of every kind of thing (a real crumb holds far more bacteria and far fewer large organisms than this), the thickness of the water film and humus coats, the pore sizes, and the nematode's width. Clay flakes are drawn at 1.8 micrometres, just under the clay limit; real clay particles can be much smaller and thinner. The scene shows a window of the crumb, not the whole crumb, which is 4 to 9 mm across in the block.

title: Sand grains
summary: Sand grains are the big mineral grains of soil, 63 micrometres to 2 millimetres across; in soils like this one they are mostly quartz.

layers.basics: These are the large, rounded lumps in the crumb. Each is a piece of rock that weathering has broken off. In most inland soils the sand is mostly quartz, because quartz does not dissolve or crumble easily and so outlasts other minerals. Sand does not hold much water or nutrients, but it gives soil its framework and its pores. The quartz crystal can be viewed from the pebble bed of the block.
layers.deeper: ISO 14688 grades sand as fine (63 to 200 micrometres), medium (200 to 630) and coarse (630 to 2,000). Silica as quartz is the most common component of sand in inland settings, because of its chemical inertness and hardness; calcium carbonate is the second most common type, and the composition is highly variable.
layers.expert: The three grains are drawn 650, 420 and 500 micrometres across, which is coarse and medium sand.

title: Silt grains
summary: Silt grains are mineral grains between 2 and 63 micrometres: too small to feel as separate grains, they give soil a smooth, floury feel.

layers.basics: Silt is the in-between size: finer than sand, coarser than clay. The grains are the small angular specks packed around the sand grains. You can feel silt as smoothness when you rub a damp soil between your fingers.
layers.deeper: On the ISO scale silt is 2 to 63 micrometres. Silt, sand and clay together make up the mineral part of the soil, and their proportions give a soil its texture.
layers.expert: The scene draws 60 grains between 14 and 40 micrometres; the number and shapes are illustrative.

title: Humus coats
summary: Humus is the dark, sticky, decayed organic matter that coats grains and helps glue crumbs together. Its molecular nature is debated.

layers.basics: The dark film on the grains in the crumb stands for humus. It is what is left of dead matter when the decomposers have taken what they can: a complex mixture, not a single substance. It helps stick the mineral grains together, holds water and nutrient ions, and gives topsoil its dark colour.
layers.deeper: The traditional view was that soil organic matter contains large, stable 'humic' molecules made in the soil. Lehmann and Kleber argued in Nature in 2015 that the evidence does not support this: they see soil organic matter as a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds, whose persistence depends largely on the soil environment. That view is itself contested, and the older textbook picture still appears in many sources. Whatever its structure, organic matter holds a great deal of nutrient charge per gram; textbook tables give a cation-exchange capacity of the order of 100 to 300 meq per 100 g for humus, usually more per gram than clay minerals. In clay-rich soils the clay supplies most of the soil's total capacity; in sandy soils the organic matter can supply most of it. Organic matter also favours aggregation by forming bridges between mineral particles.
layers.expert: The coats are drawn as thin dark shells; their thickness is illustrative. Humus is not a single molecule, so no molecule button is offered.

facts: decayed organic matter, a mixture whose molecular nature is debated

title: The water film
summary: A thin film of water coats the grains; the dissolved nutrients in it are what roots take up.

layers.basics: The grains are wet: water sticks to them in a thin film. In it are dissolved the nutrients the plants need. When the soil is moist the film is thick and the small gaps are full; when the soil dries the film thins, and the water left is held so tightly that roots cannot get it. Water is also where bacteria and nematodes swim and feed. Click the water for one of its molecules.
layers.deeper: Water that remains after drainage is the field capacity; water below the wilting point is unavailable to plants. Water is a solvent for the ions (ammonium, nitrate, potassium and so on) that plants need.
layers.expert: The film is drawn as a thin translucent coat on the big grain; its thickness (10 micrometres here) is much greater than a real film on dry soil and is only illustrative.

facts: varies with how wet the soil is

title: An air pore
summary: A pore that is not full of water is full of air: the air in soil has more carbon dioxide and less oxygen than the air above it, because roots and soil life breathe in it.

layers.basics: The dark gaps in the crumb are air pores. Roots, fungi, bacteria and animals all breathe the soil air. They use up oxygen and give off carbon dioxide, so soil air is richer in carbon dioxide than the air above ground. Click the pore to see the carbon dioxide molecule.
layers.deeper: Water and gas share the pore space; as soil wets, air is displaced; compaction reduces pore space so that air and water do not reach roots and organisms. Respiration by roots and decomposers releases carbon dioxide into the pores. Darwin noted a great excess of carbonic acid (carbon dioxide) in all soils, especially rich ones.
layers.expert: The pore is drawn as a dark lens 200 micrometres across; the sizes of real pores range widely.

facts: air: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out

title: Soil bacteria
summary: Bacteria are single-celled organisms 0.5 to 5 micrometres long; they do most of the chemical work of the soil and there are about a hundred million in a gram.

layers.basics: The tiny rods and dots on the grain surfaces are bacteria. They are the most numerous living things in soil: about a hundred million in a gram on average. They live in the film of water, feed on dead matter, and break it down: they are the chief recyclers, along with fungi. Some change nitrogen into forms plants can use. When they break down proteins they release ammonium; click one to see that molecule.
layers.deeper: Mean prokaryote density is roughly 10^8 per gram of soil, and a teaspoon of productive soil may hold 100 million to 3 billion. Microbes carry out the steps of the nitrogen cycle in soil: some bacteria fix nitrogen gas, some release ammonium from dead matter (ammonification), ammonia-oxidising archaea and bacteria and nitrite-oxidising bacteria (for example Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) turn ammonium into nitrate, and others turn nitrate back to nitrogen gas without oxygen.
layers.expert: The scene draws about 120 rods 1.6 by 3.5 micrometres; the number is far smaller than in real soil and their positions are illustrative. The bacteria are not identified by species.

title: A nematode
summary: Nematodes are microscopic roundworms, often less than 2.5 millimetres long, that graze on bacteria, fungi and other small things in the water film of the soil.

layers.basics: The long thin worm in the crumb is a nematode, a roundworm. It is not an earthworm, and it is far smaller: most free-living nematodes are less than 2.5 millimetres long and some only about a millimetre. They are very common in soil: often more than a million in a square metre, mostly in the top 15 centimetres. They swim in the film of water around the grains and eat bacteria, fungi, algae and other small things.
layers.deeper: Nematodes are very small, slender worms, bilaterally symmetrical, and often with ridges, rings or bristles on the body. The topsoil of the world holds about 4.4 × 10^20 nematodes. Some soil nematodes reach up to 7 mm.
layers.expert: The nematode is drawn 800 micrometres long and 25 micrometres wide, as a plain tube; its width and shape are illustrative.

facts: often under 2.5 mm; some ≈ 1 mm; some up to 7 mm

title: Positive ions held on clay
summary: Calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium ions cling to the negatively charged surfaces of clay plates, held loosely enough that roots and water can swap them for others.

layers.basics: The coloured balls in the scene near the clay plates are positive ions of plant nutrients: calcium (Ca²⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), potassium (K⁺) and ammonium (NH₄⁺). Each is held by the plate's negative charge, together with its shell of water molecules. They are not stuck for good: if another ion arrives in the water they can swap. This is how the clay acts as a store that releases nutrients gradually. Click an ammonium ion to see the molecule.
layers.deeper: Cations are held electrostatically in the diffuse layer, keeping their water shells, and are easily displaced by other cations in solution. Calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium are the base cations; their share of the exchange capacity is the base saturation, which indicates weathering and nutrient availability. A lower pH (more hydrogen ions) reduces variable charge, and so the capacity.
layers.expert: The ions are drawn about 200 times larger than real so that you can see them; a hydrated ion is a fraction of a nanometre across. The number, kind and place of the ions are illustrative.

facts: Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺, Na⁺, NH₄⁺ (and H⁺)

title: Nitrate in the soil water
summary: Nitrate carries a negative charge, so clay does not hold it; it stays in the water, where roots take it up and where rain can wash it away.

layers.basics: The red balls drifting away from the plates are nitrate ions, the form of nitrogen that roots take up most easily. Their charge is negative, like the clay's, so the clay pushes them away instead of holding them. This is why nitrate is easily washed out of the soil by heavy rain into streams and groundwater. Click one to see the nitrate molecule.
layers.deeper: Nitrate is highly soluble and soils are highly unable to retain anions, so it can leach to groundwater. It is made by nitrifying microbes from ammonium and can be turned back to nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria in oxygen-poor soil.
layers.expert: Ion sizes are exaggerated as on the card of the positive ions; the number and places of the nitrate ions are illustrative.

facts: taken up by roots, leached, or denitrified
